item.title: How climate change may amplify the impact of earthquakes in the Arctic
item.description: Permafrost refers to permanently frozen ground. The rock is held together by ice, much like cement binds concrete. However, when the ice thaws, the ground becomes weak and unstable. During an earthquake, this can trigger a series of natural hazards. An international research team investigated precisely such an event. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists covered 200 square metres of a Swiss glacier with sheep’s wool; early tests found...
item.description: In an innovative approach, Swiss researchers are experimenting with natural wool blankets to mitigate glacier melting. These eco-friendly coverings have shown results comparable to synthetic options during trials. The initiative makes use of discarded sheep's wool, an agricultural byproduct. Although effective in localized regions, it's important to note that this technique alone won't reverse global warming—tackling greenhouse gas emissions is essential for the long-term preservation of glaciers. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Climate and air quality are closely linked, report highlights

Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ancient charcoal reveals evidence of wildfires near the South Pole
item.description: A journey back in time to the Late Cretaceous: A swampy rainforest with conifers and tree ferns stretches as far as the eye can see, dinosaurs roam through the misty wetlands, and the climate is mild and warm. The average annual temperature is 12°C (54°F)—around two degrees higher than in present-day Germany. There is plenty of water, too, as dry periods are regularly followed by monsoon-like rainy seasons. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: In 2023, Australia put a 330-square-metre floating wetland on a wastewater lagoon
item.description: Over the course of two years, research revealed that floating wetlands successfully diminished methane emissions by sixty-six percent, alongside notable reductions in carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide levels. The native vegetation on these platforms is crucial in nurturing beneficial microbes that tackle pollutants and gases effectively. This eco-friendly treatment method reveals a significant advancement in wastewater management, with ongoing tests on analogous floating wetlands in regional agricultural dams. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: New digital tool shows exactly where California's water goes—and how climate change might disrupt it
item.description: Water has always been one of California's most contested resources. For more than a century, battles have raged over how much of the state's water should be diverted to farmland, pumped into cities or used to conserve aquatic ecosystems—and at times, these clashes have even led to violence. The state's water system consists of a dizzying array of reservoirs, rivers, dams and aqueducts, making it challenging even for experts to understand the trade-offs of different management decisions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: England released beavers into a Dorset woodland in 2025; one year later, their dams had...
item.description: Beavers newly introduced in Dorset have remarkably transformed a woodland area into a flourishing wetland. Through their natural dam-building, these creatures have slowed down water movement, resulting in the formation of deep pools. This ecological shift has rejuvenated the local fauna, reintroducing various native species to the Purbeck region. Additionally, the beaver dams serve to mitigate flooding on nearby roads during heavy rains, highlighting nature’s essential contribution to environmental resilience. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

Regions that had recorded a fall in pollution emitted by cars and industrial sites are facing new threats to air quality because of exposure to smoke from wildfires, according to a new report, while rising temperatures caused by intense heatwaves are causing a surge in ground-level ozone. item.title: Six unusual structures identified at Earth's core-mantle boundary with the help of deep learning
item.description: Since scientists can't drill 2,900 km (1,800 miles) to the boundary between Earth's core and deep mantle, they must use information relayed by seismic waves recorded during earthquakes to study this region. In a new study published in the journal JGR Solid Earth, a group of scientists used deep learning to study a large set of a specific type of seismic wave. The analysis revealed six continuous bands of irregularities at the core-mantle boundary (CMB) that had previously appeared only as sparse patches. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Johanna tiene 25 años, es universitaria, alemana, y (al igual que miles de compatriotas) una enamorada de España, país que visita con frecuencia. item.title: Air conditioners are our best bet in the fight against extreme heat – whether we like it or not
item.description: Global AC demand will inevitably accelerate as the world continues to warm amid the climate crisis The greenest campaigners against climate change have long suffered from a crippling shortcoming: they too often frame the challenge as a problem of excess consumption. This motivates calls to “degrow” the economy and to curb the population . The claim is that humans consume too many resources, which in the context of climate change means too much energy. item.title: 242 trapped by wildfire; pilots flew into flames to save them
item.description: California National Guard crews performed a historic nighttime helicopter rescue during the Creek Fire. They saved 242 people trapped by intense flames and thick smoke. This extraordinary mission utilized night-vision goggles and combat helicopters in a wildfire zone. The daring rescue demonstrated new possibilities for nighttime wildfire aviation response. California has since expanded its nighttime aviation capabilities and interagency training. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: World’s most powerful lightning-chasing satellite joins China-Nepal flood relief efforts
item.description: China is using the world’s most powerful geostationary weather satellite to track severe thunderstorms over Nepal and deliver real-time intelligence as the two countries continue search and rescue operations following last month’s devastating glacier collapse. The Fengyun‑4C satellite – launched last December and now positioned 36,000km (22,000 miles) above the equator – carries a Lightning Mapping Imager (LMI) that captures 500 frames per second, sifting through 30 gigabits of data every second... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.title: Indonesia’s most dangerous fires are burning underground
item.description: Indonesia’s dangerous peat fires are surging early in the 2026 fire season as a strengthening El Niño and severe drought dry out wetlands that can burn underground for months. These slow smoldering fires are especially destructive because they release far more fine particles and several pollutants than typical tropical forest fires, while thick smoke can make them difficult for satellites to detect. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: How discarded Christmas trees are being used to build dunes on a UK beach
item.description: Discarded Christmas trees are being used to strengthen the sand dunes at St Annes beach on England’s Fylde Coast. Since the project began in 2013, the trees have helped trap wind-blown sand and expand the dunes. The wider dunes act as a natural sea defence, helping protect nearby homes and businesses from coastal flooding while also creating habitat for specialised plants and wildlife. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: How a mountain collapse triggered Nepal’s deadly flood in just 7 minutes | The Climate Economy
item.description: How did a mountain collapse trigger one of Nepal’s deadliest flood disasters? In this explainer, we break down the strange warning signs, the shrinking river, the seismic signal initially mistaken for an earthquake, and the chain reaction that turned rock, ice and water into a catastrophic flood. Here’s what scientists know so far about the Nepal flood disaster and why experts say it could change how Himalayan hazards are monitored in the future. item.description: En Hirosaki, al norte de Japón, una compleja restauración patrimonial se ha convertido en algo bastante más insólito: miles de personas tirando de cuerdas para desplazar un castillo de cientos de toneladas. La operación utiliza una antigua técnica japonesa que permite trasladar edificios completos sin desmontarlos y ha despertado tal interés que las plazas disponibles se quedaron pequeñas. Detrás del espectáculo hay una historia que comenzó con un terremoto . Japón pidió voluntarios.
